questions.q: Why doesn't Qiskit need an equivalent of the qsharp package's Python-Q# bridge?
options: Because Qiskit does not support running on real hardware
Because Qiskit is itself a Python library -- there is no separate compiled language to bridge to, since circuit-building and execution are both just Python objects and calls
Because Qiskit circuits cannot be run more than once
Because Python cannot call any external language under any circumstances
questions.explain: Qiskit has no interop boundary because it never leaves Python -- a QuantumCircuit is a Python object built and run with Python calls. Q# is a separate statically-typed compiled language, which is why a bridge like the qsharp package is needed.

questions.q: What does the `%%qsharp` Jupyter cell magic do?
options: It converts Q# source into Qiskit Python code automatically
It lets you write and compile Q# source directly inside a notebook cell, making the defined operations callable from Python cells afterward
It only displays Q# syntax highlighting with no actual compilation
It submits the cell's contents directly to Azure Quantum hardware
questions.explain: %%qsharp compiles the Q# source in that cell; afterward, the defined operations can be called from Python via qsharp.eval(...) or similar.

questions.q: What does `qsharp.eval("PrepareAndMeasure()")` return to Python, according to the lesson?
options: A raw, unreadable binary blob requiring manual parsing
A native Python-visible value (such as the string-like Result 'Zero' or 'One') that Python code can immediately branch on, print, or store
Nothing -- it only has side effects with no return value
A full Qiskit QuantumCircuit object
questions.explain: qsharp.eval converts the Q# Result into a value Python can work with directly -- no manual serialization step is needed on the caller's part.

questions.q: For the operation that applies H to |0> and measures, what is the theoretically expected, verified probability of each outcome (Zero/One)?
options: Exactly 0.5 for each outcome, since H|0> = (|0>+|1>)/sqrt(2) gives |1/sqrt(2)|^2 = 0.5 for both amplitudes
1.0 for Zero and 0 for One
0.25 for Zero and 0.75 for One
The probability cannot be determined without running on real hardware
questions.explain: H|0> produces equal-magnitude amplitudes on |0> and |1>, each with probability exactly 0.5, verified by squaring the amplitude magnitude 1/sqrt(2).

questions.q: Why would a real 1000-shot run of the H-then-measure operation likely show counts like 501/499 rather than exactly 500/500?
options: Because the H gate is implemented incorrectly in the qsharp package
Because of ordinary sampling variation -- a finite number of shots fluctuates around the true 0.5/0.5 probability rather than landing on it exactly every time
Because Python's Counter object rounds results incorrectly
Because Azure Quantum always introduces a systematic bias toward Zero
questions.explain: A true 0.5 probability per outcome doesn't guarantee an exact 50/50 split over any finite number of shots -- random sampling naturally fluctuates around the true probability, which is expected and not an error.
